title: You are our king
hookLine: the third book opens in a clearing full of old ascetics, and the first thing they ask a prince in bark clothes is to be their king
carry: dharma: the crown goes, the duty stays

cards: Aranya means forest, and the third book, the Aranya Kanda, is the book of the forest. The forest Rama walks into now is Dandaka, the great wild country south of everything he knows. It isn't empty.
The first thing he sees, Valmiki says, is a ring of hermitages: little huts, fires burning for the daily offerings, grass laid out for rites, deer wandering without fear, birds everywhere.
Old men and women with matted hair look up from their prayers, and come out to meet him.

teach.b: The sages see Rama, Valmiki says, and can't stop looking at him: his build, his calm, his beauty, the bark clothes he wears like a king's robes. They bring fruit, roots and water, and give the travelers a hut to rest in.
Then they say something surprising. You are our king.

teach.h: YOU ARE OUR KING, CITY OR FOREST.
teach.b: Whether you live in a city or a forest, you are still the king, and a king is the one who protects.
We've given up the rod of punishment. We've given up anger. We live by our austerities, so we're like children in your care.
Protect us. Notice what's happening. Rama has just been stripped of the crown in Ayodhya.
His brother is ruling through a pair of sandals. And here, the first people he meets hand the title straight back to him. Not the palace or the throne, but the duty.

teach.h: DHARMA: THE DUTY OF YOUR PLACE.
teach.b: Hindus call this dharma: the duty that comes with who you are and where you stand.

teach.h: THE CROWN GOES. THE DUTY STAYS.
teach.b: For a kshatriya, the warrior-ruler, that duty is to protect. A promise took Rama's crown. Nothing can take his dharma.
The sages have chosen a life without weapons, and someone has to stand between them and the dark. Hold onto that request.

Much of the forest book grows out of it: the battles, the promises, even the danger that will come to Sita. It starts here, with old people in a clearing asking a young man in bark clothes to be what he was born for.

how: The Aranya Kanda, the book of the forest, opens with the sages' welcome in Dandaka, and their plea for protection runs through the book.

o: the wandering singers who first told Rama's story
the royal priests who sent Rama away from Ayodhya
the forest hermits who ask Rama to be their protector

games.q: into the forest — tap the pairs.
p: you are our king, city or forest
the sages have given it up

s: the forest of Dandaka is empty when Rama arrives
the first thing he sees is a ring of hermitages full of sages.
the sages call Rama their king though he has lost the throne
city or forest, they say, he is the king who protects.
the sages ask Rama to teach them
they ask him to protect them.

games.q: you're one of the forest sages. a young prince in bark clothes arrives with a bow. what do you ask of him?
o: to leave the forest in peace.
to protect you, as your king.
games.why: they tell him he's their king, city or forest, and ask him to protect them, since they've given up the rod. the crown went; the dharma to protect stayed.

practice: Picture a clearing in a forest, small fires, quiet people, birds, and then someone in your own life who relies on you to stand between them and trouble.
Breathe in steadiness and breathe out calm, with no need to solve anything for them right now.

wordCard.voice: The sages. The forest ascetics of Dandaka welcome Rama and ask him, king or not, to be their protector.

orig.note: Sanskrit daṇḍakāraṇya: the forest (araṇya) of Daṇḍaka, the wild country where most of the third book happens.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma, the crown goes, the duty stays. City or forest, a protector protects. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 1 (the hermitages of Dandaka; the sages' welcome and request)
